title: Study protocol for the TROG 21.08 VITaL trial: a randomized controlled trial investigating ventilation imaging to improve the quality of life for patients with lung cancer treated with radiation therapy

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Study protocol for the TROG 21.08 VITaL trial: a randomized controlled trial investigating ventilation imaging to improve the quality of life for patients with lung cancer treated with radiation therapy》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Background · abstract-1-1】Radiation therapy (RT) is indicated for 77% of patients with lung cancer. Over 20% of patients are affected by radiation-induced lung injury. Computed tomography ventilation imaging (CTVI) estimates high and low functioning lung regions. During RT planning, CTVI can guide preferential avoidance of higher ventilated regions by redirecting dose to less well ventilated regions, sparing healthy lung tissue. The double-masked randomized Trans-Tasman Radiation Oncology Group (TROG) 21.08 VITaL trial will investigate if sparing healthy lung can improve the quality of life (QoL) for patients with stage 3 non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) treated with RT.

【Introduction · p0030】Lung cancer, the leading cause of cancer mortality and disability-adjusted life years in the world [1] has a 5-year survival rate of only 28% [2]. Radiation therapy (RT) will benefit 77% of lung cancer patients and plays a central role as curative treatment in unresectable stage 3 NSCLC [3]. RT carries risks, including radiation-induced lung injury, deteriorating QoL [4] and survival [5]. Pneumonitis is the most common radiation therapy side effect, occurring more frequently in patients with stage 3 NSCLC receiving adjuvant immunotherapy where grade 2+ pneumonitis rates range from 23%–44% [6], [7], [8], [9]. A multicenter study found 86% of pneumonitis was attributable to RT, with 11% related to both RT and immunotherapy [8].

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Study protocol for the TROG 21.08 VITaL trial: a randomized controlled trial investigating ventilation imaging to improve the quality of life for patients with lung cancer treated with radiation therapy》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Study design · p0055】The study is a multicenter, prospective, double-masked, randomized controlled, two-arm, phase 3 trial, that will be conducted initially in Australia and then extended internationally. The sponsor is the University of Sydney. TROG is providing trial credentialling and quality assurance services.

【Clinical and patient outcome measures · p0110】Patient assessments will occur at baseline, weekly during RT and 1, 3, 6, 9,12, 24 and 36 months after RT treatment. These assessments will include the physician-graded toxicity using the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE v5.0), the FACT-L version 4 and local control using the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST v1.1) on follow up CT scans where available. FACT-L will be offered in multiple languages (Arabic, Chinese, English, Greek, Italian, Macedonian, Spanish, Turkish, and Vietnamese) to accommodate most primary spoken languages of patients at our recruiting sites.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Study protocol for the TROG 21.08 VITaL trial: a randomized controlled trial investigating ventilation imaging to improve the quality of life for patients with lung cancer treated with radiation therapy》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Introduction · p0030】Lung cancer, the leading cause of cancer mortality and disability-adjusted life years in the world [1] has a 5-year survival rate of only 28% [2]. Radiation therapy (RT) will benefit 77% of lung cancer patients and plays a central role as curative treatment in unresectable stage 3 NSCLC [3]. RT carries risks, including radiation-induced lung injury, deteriorating QoL [4] and survival [5]. Pneumonitis is the most common radiation therapy side effect, occurring more frequently in patients with stage 3 NSCLC receiving adjuvant immunotherapy where grade 2+ pneumonitis rates range from 23%–44% [6], [7], [8], [9]. A multicenter study found 86% of pneumonitis was attributable to RT, with 11% related to both RT and immunotherapy [8].

【Introduction · p0045】CTVI shows high and low functioning lung regions overlaid on an anatomical CT image and can generate the ventilation images from CT scans routinely acquired for lung cancer RT planning [15]. Other modalities for lung ventilation imaging include xenon CT, single photon emission CT, positron emission tomography (PET), and hyperpolarized gas magnetic resonance imaging [14], [16], [17]. One systematic review [18] (69 included studies) found moderate to strong evidence that CTVI provides the same regional ventilation information as these other modalities. A second systematic review [16] (114 included studies) proposed that further clinical studies were needed to detect differences between the anatomic and functional dose metrics. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis on the incorporation of functional lung imaging into RT planning found a 13% (95th percentiles 8%–20%) rate of grade 2+ radiation pneumonitis, with functional avoidance planning [14]. The review concluded that interventional trials related to functional lung avoidance planning are sparse, but are critical to understanding the effects on reducing toxicity and improving patient outcomes.
